quotes.t: History, despite its wrenching pain, cannot be unlived, but if faced with courage, need not be lived again.
When we give cheerfully and accept gratefully, everyone is blessed.
quotes.source: Wouldn't Take Nothing for My Journey Now

quotes.t: I've learned that you shouldn't go through life with a catcher's mitt on both hands; you need to be able to throw something back.
I object to violence because when it appears to do good, the good is only temporary; the evil it does is permanent.
There is no God higher than truth.
Anger and intolerance are the twin enemies of correct understanding.
The public is wonderfully tolerant. It forgives everything except genius.
When the gods wish to punish us, they answer our prayers.
Education is an admirable thing, but it is well to remember from time to time that nothing that is worth knowing can be taught.
In war, resolution; in defeat, defiance; in victory, magnanimity; in peace, goodwill.
I am an optimist. It does not seem to be much use being anything else.
All the great things are simple, and many can be expressed in a single word: freedom, justice, honor, duty, mercy, hope.
The Way of the warrior is the resolute acceptance of death.
It is said the warrior's is the twofold Way of pen and sword, and he should have a taste for both.
In the void is virtue, and no evil.
Security is mostly a superstition. It does not exist in nature, nor do the children of men as a whole experience it.
When we do the best we can, we never know what miracle is wrought in our life, or in the life of another.
Everything has its wonders, even darkness and silence, and I learn, whatever state I may be in, therein to be content.
All men can see these tactics whereby I conquer, but what none can see is the strategy out of which victory is evolved.
The general who advances without coveting fame and retreats without fearing disgrace, whose only thought is to protect his country and do good service for his sovereign, is the jewel of the kingdom.
The quality of decision is like the well-timed swoop of a falcon which enables it to strike and destroy its victim.
Whatever you think, that you will be. If you think yourselves weak, weak you will be; if you think yourselves strong, strong you will be.
Each work has to pass through these stages — ridicule, opposition, and then acceptance. Those who think ahead of their time are sure to be misunderstood.
Dare to be free, dare to go as far as your thought leads, and dare to carry that out in your life.
Be active! Take on responsibility! Work for the things you believe in. If you do not, you are surrendering your fate to others.
Science is global. Technology must be for common people.
Life is a difficult game. You can win it only by retaining your birthright to be a person.
You can have it all. Just not all at once.
Create the highest, grandest vision possible for your life, because you become what you believe.
Challenges are gifts that force us to search for a new center of gravity. Don't fight them. Just find a new way to stand.
Do not stop thinking of life as an adventure. You have no security unless you can live bravely, excitingly, imaginatively; unless you can choose a challenge instead of competence.
I believe that anyone can conquer fear by doing the things he fears to do, provided he keeps doing them until he gets a record of successful experiences behind him.
It is a brave thing to have courage to be an individual; it is also, perhaps, a lonely thing. But it is better than not being an individual, which is to be nobody at all.
Wisdom is the daughter of experience.
The human foot is a masterpiece of engineering and a work of art.
He who does not punish evil commands it to be done.
Despair is the conclusion of fools.
The magic of first love is our ignorance that it can ever end.
To be conscious that you are ignorant of the facts is a great step to knowledge.
We never live, but we hope to live; and as we are always arranging to be happy, it is inevitable that we should never be so.
Men never do evil so completely and cheerfully as when they do it from religious conviction.
There are only two kinds of men: the righteous who think they are sinners and the sinners who think they are righteous.
Youth has no age.
If I don't have red, I use blue.
It is your work in life that is the ultimate seduction.
The surest way to corrupt a youth is to instruct him to hold in higher esteem those who think alike than those who think differently.
The advantage of a bad memory is that one enjoys several times the same good things for the first time.
One repays a teacher badly if one always remains nothing but a pupil.
The greatest glory in living lies not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall.
If you want to make peace with your enemy, you have to work with your enemy. Then he becomes your partner.
People must learn to hate, and if they can learn to hate, they can be taught to love, for love comes more naturally to the human heart than its opposite.
What can you do to promote world peace? Go home and love your family.
I know God will not give me anything I can't handle. I just wish that He didn't trust me so much.
The most terrible poverty is loneliness and the feeling of being unloved.
To love is to act.
Nothing makes a man so adventurous as an empty pocket.
A garden to walk in and immensity to dream in — what more could he ask? A few flowers at his feet and above him the stars.
Nobody realizes that some people expend tremendous energy merely to be normal.
There is no fate that cannot be surmounted by scorn.
Real generosity toward the future lies in giving all to the present.
I'm just sitting here watching the wheels go round and round, I really love to watch them roll.
There is no love sincerer than the love of food.
No one loves the messenger who brings bad news.
The first step in the evolution of ethics is a sense of solidarity with other human beings.
The greatest danger occurs at the moment of victory.
Compassion is not a relationship between the healer and the wounded. It's a relationship between equals.
When you ride in a boat and watch the shore, you might assume that the shore is moving. But when you keep your eyes closely on the boat, you can see that the boat moves.
If you have built castles in the air, your work need not be lost; that is where they should be. Now put the foundations under them.
When the winds of change blow, some people build walls and others build windmills.
Without peace, all other dreams vanish and are reduced to ashes.
Justice means minding your own business and not meddling with other men's concerns.
The greatest good of a man is daily to converse about virtue.
Doubt is not a pleasant condition, but certainty is absurd.
quotes.source: Letter to Frederick William, Prince of Prussia (1770)

quotes.t: There is nothing in the world so irresistibly contagious as laughter and good-humour.
If your nerve, deny you, go above your nerve.
You may delay, but time will not.
The arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends toward justice.
quotes.source: Remaining Awake Through a Great Revolution, sermon (1968)

quotes.t: There is nothing I would not do for those who are really my friends. I have no notion of loving people by halves; it is not my nature.
We can know only that we know nothing. And that is the highest degree of human wisdom.

Love never dies a natural death. It dies because we don't know how to replenish its source. It dies of blindness and errors and betrayals. It dies of illness and wounds; it dies of weariness, of witherings, of tarnishings.
quotes.source: The Diary of Anais Nin, Vol. 4 (1944-1947)

quotes.t: In the long run, the sharpest weapon of all is a kind and gentle spirit.
quotes.source: The Diary of a Young Girl

quotes.t: It is not the brains that matter most, but that which guides them — the character, the heart, generous qualities, progressive ideas.
A person is a person through other persons.
Practice is the best of all instructors.
No great man lives in vain. The history of the world is but the biography of great men.
quotes.source: On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History (1841)

quotes.t: Only the person who has experienced light and darkness, war and peace, rise and fall, only that person has truly experienced life.
Cowardice is the most terrible of vices.
Only those who will risk going too far can possibly find out just how far one can go.
Think where man's glory most begins and ends, and say my glory was I had such friends.
If I had to choose between betraying my country and betraying my friend I hope I should have the guts to betray my country.
Wisdom tells me I am nothing. Love tells me I am everything. And between the two my life flows.
Any sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic.
The curious paradox is that when I accept myself just as I am, then I can change.
Someone will remember us, I say, even in another time.
A dead thing can go with the stream, but only a living thing can go against it.
The belief in a supernatural source of evil is not necessary; men alone are quite capable of every wickedness.
What you see and what you hear depends a great deal on where you are standing. It also depends on what sort of person you are.
When I get a little money I buy books; and if any is left I buy food and clothes.
I never saw a wild thing sorry for itself. A small bird will drop frozen dead from a bough without ever having felt sorry for itself.
Stand a little less between me and the sun.
quotes.source: Diogenes Laërtius, Lives of Eminent Philosophers

A.P.J. Abdul Kalam.bio: Indian aerospace scientist and the 11th President of India (2002-2007), known as the 'Missile Man of India'.

Albert Camus.bio: French-Algerian writer and philosopher, author of The Stranger; Nobel Prize in Literature 1957.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Anais Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin, French-born American diarist and novelist. She is celebrated for her multi-volume Diary, begun when she was eleven, and for works such as Delta of Venus.

Anne Frank.bio: German-born Jewish diarist whose diary documents life in hiding during the Holocaust.

Arthur C. Clarke.bio: British science-fiction writer (1917–2008), author of 2001: A Space Odyssey.

Benjamin Disraeli.bio: British statesman who served twice as Prime Minister and led the Conservative Party. He was also a successful novelist, writing books such as Coningsby and Sybil.
Benjamin Disraeli.credit: Cornelius Jabez Hughes, Public domain (File: File:Benjamin Disraeli, Earl of Beaconsfield.jpg)

Benjamin Franklin.bio: American polymath - printer, scientist, diplomat - and a Founding Father of the United States.

Blaise Pascal.bio: French mathematician, physicist and philosopher, author of the Pensées.
Blaise Pascal.credit: unknown; a copy of the painting of François II Quesnel, which was made for Gérard Edelinck en 1691, Public domain

C. S. Lewis.bio: C. S. Lewis was an Irish-born scholar and writer at Oxford, author of The Chronicles of Narnia, Mere Christianity and The Screwtape Letters. A close friend of Tolkien, he moved from atheism to Christianity and became one of its most popular modern interpreters.

Carl Rogers.bio: American psychologist (1902–1987), a founder of humanistic psychology and person-centred therapy.

Charles Dickens.bio: English novelist and social critic; author of A Christmas Carol, Oliver Twist and Great Expectations.

D.H. Lawrence.bio: English novelist and poet (1885–1930), author of Sons and Lovers and Lady Chatterley's Lover.

Desiderius Erasmus.bio: Dutch Renaissance humanist, author of In Praise of Folly.
Desiderius Erasmus.credit: Attributed to Lucas Cranach the Elder, Public domain

Desmond Tutu.bio: South African Anglican archbishop and Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1984) who campaigned against apartheid.

Diogenes.bio: Greek philosopher (c. 412–323 BCE), one of the founders of Cynicism.

Dogen.bio: Founder of the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan and author of the Shōbōgenzō, a landmark of Buddhist philosophy.

E. M. Forster.bio: Edward Morgan Forster was an English novelist known for A Room with a View, Howards End and A Passage to India, works examining class and connection in Edwardian society.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.
Eleanor Roosevelt.credit: Unknown authorUnknown author, Public domain (File: Eleanor Roosevelt portrait 1933.jpg)

Emily Dickinson.bio: American poet whose nearly 1,800 poems, mostly unpublished in her lifetime, made her a central figure of American literature.
Emily Dickinson.credit: Miscellaneous Items in High Demand, PPOC, Library of Congress, Public domain

Friedrich Nietzsche.bio: German philosopher known for Thus Spoke Zarathustra and the concept of the will to power.

Fyodor Dostoevsky.bio: Russian novelist, author of Crime and Punishment and The Brothers Karamazov.

G. K. Chesterton.bio: Gilbert Keith Chesterton was an English writer, philosopher and critic whose work ranged from the Father Brown detective stories to theology and social commentary. His wit and paradox made him one of the most quoted writers of his era.

George Bernard Shaw.bio: Irish playwright and critic; author of Pygmalion; Nobel Prize in Literature 1925.
George Bernard Shaw.credit: Sussman, Public domain (File: George Bernard Shaw, playwright (SAYRE 9001).jpg)

Helen Keller.bio: American author and activist who, deaf and blind from childhood, became a renowned advocate for disability rights.
Helen Keller.credit: Los Angeles Times; restored by User:Rhododendrites, Public domain

Henry David Thoreau.bio: American writer known for Walden (1854) and the essay Civil Disobedience.

Jane Austen.bio: English novelist known for Pride and Prejudice and Emma, celebrated for irony and social observation.
Jane Austen.credit: Engraving by William Home Lizars after James Andrews, Public domain

Jawaharlal Nehru.bio: Leader of India's independence movement and the country's first Prime Minister (1947-1964).

John Lennon.bio: English singer-songwriter, co-founder of the Beatles and solo artist known for Imagine.

Joseph Conrad.bio: Polish-British novelist (1857–1924), author of Heart of Darkness and Lord Jim.

Leo Tolstoy.bio: Russian novelist, author of War and Peace and Anna Karenina.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.
Leonardo da Vinci.credit: Leonardo da Vinci, Public domain (File: Leonardo self.jpg)

Mahatma Gandhi.bio: Leader of India's nonviolent independence movement; pioneered satyagraha and became the father of the Indian nation.

Martin Luther King Jr..bio: American Baptist minister who led the civil rights movement; Nobel Peace Prize laureate 1964.

Maya Angelou.bio: American poet and memoirist best known for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969).
Maya Angelou.credit: Bee Photos by Ryan Marty, Public domain

Mikhail Bulgakov.bio: Russian writer (1891–1940), author of the novel The Master and Margarita.

Miyamoto Musashi.bio: Legendary Japanese swordsman, undefeated in over sixty duels, author of The Book of Five Rings and the Dokkodo.

Mother Teresa.bio: Albanian-Indian Catholic nun who founded the Missionaries of Charity in Kolkata; Nobel Peace Prize laureate (1979).
Mother Teresa.credit: John Mathew Smith & www.celebrity-photos.com from Laurel  Maryland, USA, CC BY-SA 2.0

Napoleon Bonaparte.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte was a French military leader who rose to prominence during the French Revolution and became Emperor of the French in 1804. His Napoleonic Wars reshaped Europe, and his Napoleonic Code influenced legal systems worldwide. He died in exile on Saint Helena.

Nelson Mandela.role: Anti-apartheid leader, President of South Africa
Nelson Mandela.bio: South African anti-apartheid revolutionary who spent 27 years in prison and became the country's first Black president in 1994.

Nisargadatta Maharaj.bio: Indian spiritual teacher (1897–1981), known for the book of talks I Am That.

Oprah Winfrey.bio: American talk-show host and media executive whose long-running show made her one of the most influential broadcasters in history.
Oprah Winfrey.credit: US Embassy South Africa, Public domain

Oscar Wilde.bio: Irish playwright, poet and author of The Picture of Dorian Gray, famed for his wit and epigrams.
Oscar Wilde.credit: Napoleon Sarony (restoration by Adam Cuerden), Public domain

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.
Pablo Picasso.credit: Didier Descouens, Public domain (File: File:(Barcelona) Retrat de Picasso - Pablo Gargallo - Museu Nacional d'Art de Catalunya.jpg)

Pema Chodron.bio: Pema Chodron is an American nun in the Tibetan Buddhist tradition and a widely read author and teacher. Her books, including When Things Fall Apart, bring Buddhist teachings on compassion and difficulty to a broad audience.

Plato.bio: Greek philosopher, student of Socrates and author of The Republic.

Publilius Syrus.bio: Publilius Syrus was a Latin writer of the 1st century BC who was brought to Italy as a slave from Syria and later freed. He is known for his Sententiae, a collection of moral maxims drawn from his mimes.

Sappho.bio: Greek lyric poet (c. 630 – c. 570 BCE) from the island of Lesbos, one of the great lyric poets of antiquity.

Socrates.bio: Greek philosopher of Athens, central figure of Western philosophy; left no writings.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Stefan Zweig.bio: Austrian writer (1881–1942), author of the memoir The World of Yesterday and the novella Chess Story; one of the most widely translated writers of his time.

Sun Tzu.bio: Ancient Chinese general traditionally credited with The Art of War, a treatise on strategy studied worldwide for over two thousand years.
Sun Tzu.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: 吴司马孙武.jpg)

Swami Vivekananda.bio: Indian Hindu monk who introduced Vedanta and Yoga to the West; famous for his 1893 Chicago Parliament of Religions address.
Swami Vivekananda.credit: Unknown author, Public domain (File: Swami Vivekananda at Parliament of Religions.jpg)

T. S. Eliot.bio: Thomas Stearns Eliot, known as T. S. Eliot, was an American-born British poet and critic, author of The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock, The Waste Land and Four Quartets. He received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1948 and is regarded as a central figure of modernist poetry.

Thomas Carlyle.bio: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish historian, philosopher and essayist whose works, including Sartor Resartus and On Heroes, Hero-Worship, and the Heroic in History, shaped Victorian thought. His history of the French Revolution is regarded as a classic of the genre.

Victor Hugo.bio: French poet and novelist, author of Les Misérables and The Hunchback of Notre-Dame.
Victor Hugo.credit: Étienne Carjat, Public domain (File: Victor Hugo by Étienne Carjat 1876 - full.jpg)

Voltaire.bio: Voltaire, born François-Marie Arouet, was a French Enlightenment writer, philosopher and historian famous for the novella Candide and for his witty defence of civil liberties, including freedom of speech and religion. He was one of the most prolific and influential writers of his age.

W. B. Yeats.bio: William Butler Yeats was an Irish poet and a driving force of the Irish literary revival, co-founding Dublin's Abbey Theatre. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923, and poems such as The Second Coming and Sailing to Byzantium rank among the greatest of the 20th century.

Winston Churchill.bio: British prime minister during the Second World War and Nobel laureate in Literature.
